passage: On the last night of the winter holidays, Yusuf finally took out the science project sheet: a model of a volcano, due tomorrow. "Ten minutes," he told his brother Tejas. "Just some clay and paint." Tejas raised an eyebrow. "Your solar system took the whole Diwali weekend." "That was different. Planets are round." The stationery shop downstairs had its shutter down for the holiday, so there was no clay. Yusuf mixed flour and water instead. It was sticky and kept sliding off the bottle. Then the power went out. By candlelight, with Ammi holding the torch, the volcano leaned sideways like a sleepy dog. At eleven, Yusuf was still painting and yawning, quite sure that next time it really would take ten minutes.

qa.q: What was Yusuf's science project?
qa.a: A model of a volcano, due tomorrow.

qa.q: Why did Yusuf believe the volcano would take ten minutes?
qa.a: He pictured the easy version, just clay and paint, and felt confident and hopeful, forgetting how long the solar system model had taken.

qa.q: What could Yusuf try with his next project?
qa.a: Remember how long the last model really took, check early what materials he needs, and start several days before it is due.

qa.q: How does Tejas see Yusuf's ten-minute plan?
qa.a: Tejas is doubtful and a bit amused, remembering that the solar system took the whole Diwali weekend.

grounding: Shows a child saying a project will be quick and starting the night before, imagining the ideal path and forgetting past delays.

passage:
Saturday morning, the week after Holi.
"Didi, don't worry. I'll finish the whole chemistry syllabus this weekend."
"Fourteen chapters, Nandini?" Vandana didi looked up from her laptop.
"Seven today, seven tomorrow. Easy."
"Last term you took four days for the organic chapters alone."
"That's because I had no plan then. Now I have a timetable." Nandini waved a chart coloured in six highlighters.
Sunday, ten at night.
"Didi, I've only done three."
"Three chapters?"
"I don't get it! I planned every hour. But the numericals took forever, and I kept checking answers, and then lunch, and..." Her voice cracked. "How did it take so long?"
"The same way it did last term."
"So what do I do? The test is Friday!"
"Tomorrow we time one chapter properly. Then we plan again, with real numbers."

qa.q: How many chapters had Nandini finished by Sunday night?
qa.a: Only three chapters.

qa.q: How did Nandini feel on Sunday night, and why?
qa.a: She felt shocked and upset, because her bright plan of seven chapters a day ignored how long chapters had taken her before.

qa.q: What would you advise Nandini for the new plan?
qa.a: Time one chapter honestly, use that and last term's experience to plan, and spread revision over more days with some slack.

qa.q: How does Vandana didi see the weekend plan from the start?
qa.a: Vandana is doubtful from the start, remembering the four days the organic chapters took, but stays kind and practical when the plan falls apart.

grounding: Shows a teenager planning to revise a whole syllabus in a weekend and being shocked when it takes far longer, having ignored past experience.

passage:
After Durga Puja, October: Binita pinned the thesis deadline, January 5, above her desk and laughed at it. "Interviews in two weeks, writing in two more. I'll be done by December." Uma, who had started in August, only said, "Transcribing takes ages."
Early December: Just six of the fifteen interviews were done. Each hour of recording took Binita four hours to type out. The fog made the morning bus late, and two farmers cancelled. She stopped going to the canteen.
January 4, near midnight: Binita sat on the hostel floor surrounded by printouts, chapter four still empty, fingers trembling over the keyboard. She called Uma, crying. "How did it take so long? I had a plan." Uma came over with her own laptop and a flask of tea, and they worked side by side until the sky outside turned grey.

qa.q: How many interviews were done by early December?
qa.a: Just six of the fifteen interviews were done.

qa.q: Why did Binita laugh at the deadline in October?
qa.a: She pictured the best-case story, two weeks of interviews and two of writing, and felt confident and relaxed, not counting on transcribing, fog or cancellations.

qa.q: What could Binita have done differently in October?
qa.a: She could have asked Uma or her supervisor how long each thesis step usually takes, broken the work into parts, and added extra time for delays.

qa.q: What is the last night like for Uma?
qa.a: Uma, who had warned about transcribing, stays up till dawn helping, probably tired but caring rather than saying she was right.

grounding: Shows a student underestimating a thesis and panicking near the deadline because it took far longer than the best-case plan.

passage:
Monday: Yash, who ran three bakeries in Nagpur, asked Vishal how soon the new ordering website could be ready. "Two weeks?" Yash said hopefully. Vishal didn't answer on the spot. "Give me until Wednesday."
Wednesday: Vishal opened his old project notes. His last three similar sites had taken five, six and seven weeks, not the four he had guessed each time. He broke the job into eight parts, estimated each one, and added a buffer for the payment page, which had held him up twice before. Then he called Yash. "Seven weeks, and I'll show you progress every Friday." Yash sighed but agreed.
Seven weeks later: The payment page did get stuck, for nine days. The site still went live on the promised Friday. Yash brought a box of warm croissants to Vishal's desk and asked him to quote for the next project too.

qa.q: How long had Vishal's last three similar sites taken?
qa.a: Five, six and seven weeks.

qa.q: Why did Vishal avoid answering Yash on the spot?
qa.a: Vishal seemed careful and a little wary of his own hopeful guesses, knowing he had underestimated similar sites before.

qa.q: Which steps made Vishal's estimate reliable?
qa.a: Checking how long past sites really took, breaking the job into eight parts, and adding a buffer for the payment page before promising a date.

qa.q: How did Yash feel when the site went live on the promised Friday?
qa.a: Yash, who had sighed at seven weeks, felt pleased and grateful enough to bring croissants, because the date held despite the nine-day delay.

grounding: Shows a worker checking how long similar tasks really took, breaking the job into parts and adding a buffer before promising dates.

passage:
Subject: Re: my team keeps missing dates
Hi Nitin,
I read your note about your team being "lazy" with deadlines. I felt exactly the same last year. Then I pulled up our old sprint sheets. Every single person, me included, had guessed short. Farah said three days for the report module; it took seven. Deepak said a week for testing; it took twelve days. Nobody was slacking. They were imagining the smooth version, the way people do.
So I changed two things. First, I ask for a range now: best case, likely, worst case. Second, once a month we look at how our past guesses compared with what actually happened. No blame, just the numbers. Our missed dates have roughly halved since March.
Try it for one sprint? I'm happy to sit in on your planning.
Sarika

qa.q: How long did the report module take compared with Farah's guess?
qa.a: Farah said three days, and it took seven.

qa.q: What did Sarika feel about missed deadlines before looking at the old sheets?
qa.a: Sarika felt frustrated, much like Nitin now, until the sheets showed everyone guessing short rather than slacking.

qa.q: What two changes does Sarika suggest, and why do they work?
qa.a: Asking for best, likely and worst-case ranges, and reviewing past guesses monthly without blame, because they correct hopeful estimates instead of blaming people.

qa.q: How might Farah and Deepak feel under Sarika's new approach?
qa.a: They are likely relieved and more honest, since giving a range and checking past guesses is treated as learning, not as proof of laziness.

grounding: Shows a lead treating repeated optimistic dates as a pattern of human thinking rather than laziness, asking for ranges and reviewing past accuracy.

passage: During the Teej fair in Bundi, a big screen beside the temple played clips of a famous local singer who had left school at fifteen and now sang in big cities. Jaya watched, clapping. "She never finished class ten, and look at her," she told her cousin Payal. "Rohit bhaiya dropped out too, and he owns a phone shop now. School is just a waste of time." Payal licked her kulfi. "What about the ten other boys from his batch who dropped out? Where are they?" "Who cares? They weren't talented." Jaya was already planning: skip the half-yearly exams, practise singing on the roof, upload videos. The only dropouts she could name were the ones on screens and shop signboards; the rest had simply vanished from her view.

qa.q: Where was the big screen playing the singer's clips?
qa.a: Beside the temple, during the Teej fair in Bundi.

qa.q: Why does Jaya feel sure school is a waste of time?
qa.a: She feels excited and inspired, because the only dropouts she can picture are the singer and Rohit bhaiya, who both did well.

qa.q: What question could help Jaya before she skips her exams?
qa.a: She could ask where all the other dropouts are now, like the ten boys Payal mentions, and talk with a teacher or parent about keeping school while practising singing.

qa.q: How does Payal see Jaya's plan?
qa.a: Payal is doubtful, thinking of the many dropouts nobody sees, and is probably worried that Jaya is judging only from the winners.

grounding: Shows a teenager who sees only successful dropouts and concludes the path is easy, never noticing those who tried and quietly failed.

passage:
Dear Maria,
Happy New Year from a very cold Dehradun! I've made big changes and wanted you to hear first.
All winter I've been reading about famous founders, and they share the same habits: up at 4 am, cold showers, sixteen-hour workdays, skipping classes that "waste time." One of them even dropped out in second year. So I'm doing all of it. My alarm has been set for 4 am since Monday. I've stopped going to statistics. If it made them rich, it has to work, right?
My roommate says loads of people wake at 4 and still fail; you just never hear about them. I told him that's exactly what people who don't try would say.
Write soon and tell me everything about Lisbon.
Tanvir

qa.q: What time has Tanvir's alarm been set for since Monday?
qa.a: 4 am.

qa.q: Why does Tanvir feel sure the founders' habits will work?
qa.a: He feels inspired and hopeful, because every story he reads is about someone who succeeded, so the habits look like the cause of success.

qa.q: What could Tanvir ask before copying the habits?
qa.a: He could ask how many people had the same habits and failed, keep going to statistics, and try one change at a time.

qa.q: How does Tanvir's roommate see the plan?
qa.a: The roommate thinks the stories hide everyone who woke at 4 and still failed, and is sceptical about copying them.

grounding: Shows a student copying famous founders' habits without noticing the many people with the same habits who failed.

passage:
Supervisor's note, 3 July
Minakshi came in excited about a tuition centre that wanted our scholarship partnership: its brochure showed forty smiling toppers from last year. Nandini, who reviews our partners, read it twice and asked a quiet question: "Forty toppers out of how many students? And where are the rest?" Minakshi admitted she didn't know. Nandini wrote to the centre asking for the full batch results, including students who left mid-year. The reply took two weeks: the batch had started with over four hundred, and nearly a third had left before the exam. We didn't reject the centre, but we asked for a small trial with our own students, tracking every one of them. I've asked Nandini to add "Who is missing?" to our partner checklist.

qa.q: How many toppers did the brochure show?
qa.a: Forty smiling toppers from last year.

qa.q: What does Nandini's quiet question suggest about her state of mind?
qa.a: She seems curious and calmly cautious, not swept up by the smiling faces, wanting to see the whole group before feeling impressed.

qa.q: Why was asking for the full batch results a wise step?
qa.a: It showed that the batch began with over four hundred and nearly a third left, so the forty toppers were a small, selected part of the story.

qa.q: How might Minakshi feel after the centre's reply?
qa.a: Minakshi may feel a little embarrassed about the early excitement, but also glad the team checked before committing.

grounding: Shows a thoughtful person asking where the failures are and what the whole group looked like before praising a course.

passage: At the city engineering office, the tea break turned into a speech. Uday sir tapped the framed photo of the old clock tower on the wall. "They built properly in those days. Look, still standing after a hundred years. Today's buildings crack in ten." Two juniors nodded. Harish, six months into the job, had spent the morning in the archive room with the old ward registers. He had seen page after page of buildings from the same decades marked "collapsed", "demolished", "unsafe". Hundreds of them. Only the strongest had lasted long enough to be photographed and admired. He hesitated, then said, "Sir, the registers list a lot of old buildings that fell down. We only see the ones that didn't." Uday sir frowned, then pulled the register towards him and turned the pages slowly.

qa.q: Which building did Uday sir point to?
qa.a: The old clock tower in the framed photo on the wall.

qa.q: What was Harish feeling before he spoke up?
qa.a: Harish felt hesitant and a bit nervous about correcting a senior, but also sure of what the registers showed.

qa.q: What made Harish's comment persuasive?
qa.a: He used evidence from the old ward registers, the many buildings marked collapsed or demolished, instead of simply arguing.

qa.q: Why might Uday sir believe old buildings were better made?
qa.a: Uday sir sees only the old buildings still standing, like the clock tower, while the weaker ones are gone, so the survivors look typical.

grounding: Shows a young professional hearing that old buildings were better made and noting that only the durable ones remain to be seen.

passage: In the week of Makar Sankranti, every child in Yash's lane in a village near Nashik seemed to own the same shiny plastic spinning top from the fair. Yash had always loved his wooden lattu, the one Aaba carved from mango wood. But when Sunaina and the others spun their plastic tops in a ring, nobody looked at his. "Wood is old-fashioned," someone said. That evening Yash told Aai he hated his lattu. He begged for twenty rupees and bought the same plastic top. It wobbled and fell over almost every time. Still, he stood in the ring with the others, grinning, while the wooden lattu lay in a corner of the cowshed, forgotten.

qa.q: Who carved Yash's wooden lattu?
qa.a: Aaba carved it from mango wood.

qa.q: Why did Yash suddenly say he hated his lattu?
qa.a: He felt left out when nobody looked at his wooden top, so fitting in with the group mattered more to him than what he actually liked.

qa.q: How could Aai or Aaba help Yash?
qa.a: They could ask what he really enjoys about each top, and suggest he show the others how the wooden lattu spins, so he can belong without giving up what he likes.

qa.q: How might Aaba feel seeing the lattu forgotten in the cowshed?
qa.a: Aaba may feel a little sad and hurt that the top he carved was put aside for a plastic one.

grounding: Shows a child wanting the top everyone has and changing his taste to fit in, even though he liked his own better.
